introduction: This foundational level defines the three distinct pillars of legal writing. It strictly focuses on the Golden Rules of Pleading under Order VI of the CPC, distinguishing between what a lawyer must reveal in court and what they must hold back for trial.

core_concepts.title: Defining the Three Pillars
core_concepts.description:
1. Drafting: The general practice of writing any legal document (e.g., contracts, notices, company resolutions).
2. Pleading: The formal written statements filed in a Court of law by the parties to a case (i.e., Plaint by the Plaintiff, and Written Statement by the Defendant).
3. Conveyancing: The specialized drafting of legal instruments that transfer property rights from one living person to another (e.g., Sale Deeds, Leases, Mortgages).

core_concepts.title: The Four Golden Rules of Pleading (Order VI, Rule 2 CPC)
core_concepts.description:
The absolute bedrock of civil litigation drafting. Every pleading MUST follow these four rules:
1. Plead Facts, not Law: Do not write 'The defendant is liable under Section 73 of the Contract Act'. State the facts of the breach; the judge will apply the law.
2. Plead Material Facts (Facta Probanda): You must state the essential facts that constitute your cause of action.
3. Do NOT plead Evidence (Facta Probantia): You must not write the evidence by which the facts are to be proved. (e.g., State 'A was driving at 100 km/h'. Do NOT state 'B saw A driving at 100 km/h and will testify to it').
4. Be Concise: The facts must be stated in a concise form, divided into numbered paragraphs.

core_concepts.title: Verification of Pleadings (Order VI, Rule 15)
core_concepts.description:
A pleading has no legal value unless verified.
- The Rule: Every pleading must be verified at the foot by the party (or someone acquainted with the facts). The party must explicitly state which paragraphs they verify from their own direct knowledge, and which they verify based on information received and believed to be true. 
- Consequence: False verification is punishable as the crime of perjury under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).

core_concepts.title: Deed vs. Agreement
core_concepts.description:
- Agreement: A meeting of minds where an offer is accepted and supported by consideration. It creates obligations but doesn't necessarily transfer ownership immediately.
- Deed: A formal, written, signed, attested, and usually registered instrument that confirms, creates, or transfers an interest, right, or property (e.g., transferring the actual title of a house).

important_entities.name: Alternative and Inconsistent Pleadings
important_entities.key_fact: You can plead alternative facts, but not mutually destructive ones.
important_entities.significance: A plaintiff can plead alternative grounds for relief (e.g., 'I am the owner by purchase; OR alternatively, I am the owner by adverse possession'). However, one cannot plead entirely mutually destructive/inconsistent facts (e.g., 'I was never at the scene of the crime, AND I hit the victim in self-defense').

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
Examiners will ask: 'Does Order VI Rule 2 allow a party to plead Facta Probantia?' **NO**. 
- *Facta Probanda* = The facts to be proved (Material facts - MUST be pleaded).
- *Facta Probantia* = The facts by which the material facts are to be proved (Evidence - STRICTLY BANNED from pleadings).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: F M N C (Facts, Material, No Evidence, Concise)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Before drafting any plaint in a Judiciary exam, ensure it passes the FMNC test.

exam_strategy_tips: In Judiciary Mains, if you are asked to draft a Plaint, you MUST end it with the Verification clause and the date/place of drafting. Failing to include the Verification clause will cost you 20-30% of the total marks.
